1  high  A local account with a login shell has no password (ubuntu) [accounts.empty_password]
   Observed      accounts.passwd_status#1 (07:12, as deploy (sudo -n)): name=ops status=NP
   Observed      accounts.passwd#1 (07:12, as deploy): name=ops uid=1001 shell=/bin/bash
   Severity      high
   Why here      capped at high by data_matters_most: critical means that anyone, or someone with no
                 right to it, can use this now, or that you believe it is handled; data_matters_most
                 says neither.
   Fix           Lock the account, or set a password if a person really logs in with one.
                 Caveat: Find out what the account is for before you change it. Locking stops
                   password logins only; with UsePAM no in sshd it also blocks SSH key logins for
                   that account.
                 Commands (review before running):
                   # who is it, and does anyone use it?
                   sudo passwd -S <account>
                   last <account> | head
                   # nobody logs in with a password: lock it
                   sudo passwd -l <account>
                   # a service account that should never log in: also
                   sudo usermod -s /usr/sbin/nologin <account>
                   # a person who needs it: set one
                   sudo passwd <account>
                   # confirm sshd refuses empty passwords (expect "permitemptypasswords no")
                   sudo sshd -T | grep -i permitemptypasswords

2  high  /etc/shadow has an unexpected mode (ubuntu) [accounts.shadow_permissions_unexpected]
   Observed      accounts.shadow_meta#1 (07:12, as deploy): -rw-r--rw-:646:root:shadow
   Severity      high
   Why here      scheck was not told how this machine is used (for example, whether it faces the
                 internet), so this is the standard rating.
   Fix           Restore the mode this distribution ships.
                 Caveat: Match the distribution's own default rather than copying a mode from
                   another system.
                 Commands (review before running):
                   stat -c '%A %a %U:%G' /etc/shadow
                   # Debian and Ubuntu: 640 root:shadow — Fedora and RHEL: 000 root:root

3  high  sshd accepts password authentication (ubuntu) [sshd.password_auth_enabled]
   Observed      sshd.config#1 (07:12, as deploy (sudo -n)): passwordauthentication yes
   Severity      high: base medium, +1 data matters most (data.matters_most[0])
   Why here      You listed ubuntu under data.matters_most as holding customer orders, so this ranks
                 one step higher.
   Fix           Set PasswordAuthentication no and rely on key authentication.
                 Caveat: Confirm at least one working key-based login first, from a second session,
                   or you will lock yourself out.
                 Commands (review before running):
                   # review the effective configuration first:
                   sudo sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication
                   # then set PasswordAuthentication no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config or a file in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/
                   sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload sshd

4  high  sshd permits direct root login (ubuntu) [sshd.root_login_enabled]
   Observed      sshd.config#1 (07:12, as deploy (sudo -n)): permitrootlogin yes
   Severity      high
   Why here      capped at high by data_matters_most: critical means that anyone, or someone with no
                 right to it, can use this now, or that you believe it is handled; data_matters_most
                 says neither.
   Fix           Set PermitRootLogin no and log in as a user who escalates with sudo.
                 Caveat: Make sure an unprivileged account with sudo rights can log in first.
                   `prohibit-password` still allows key-based root login.
                 Commands (review before running):
                   # set PermitRootLogin no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config or a file in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/
                   sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload sshd

5  medium  World-writable paths without the sticky bit (ubuntu) [fs.world_writable_present]
   Observed      fs.world_writable#1 (07:12, as deploy): /opt/app/uploads
   Severity      medium
   Why here      scheck was not told how this machine is used (for example, whether it faces the
                 internet), so this is the standard rating.
   Fix           Review each path and remove world write where it is not deliberate.
                 Caveat: Shared directories that are world-writable by design (/tmp, /var/tmp) carry
                   the sticky bit and are already excluded from this check.
                 Commands (review before running):
                   # review first:
                   ls -ld <path>
                   sudo chmod o-w <path>

6  medium  SELinux is disabled (ubuntu) [mac.selinux_disabled]
   Observed      mac.sestatus#1 (07:12, as deploy): SELinux status: disabled
   Severity      medium
   Why here      scheck was not told how this machine is used (for example, whether it faces the
                 internet), so this is the standard rating.
   Fix           Set SELINUX=enforcing in /etc/selinux/config, relabel, and reboot.
                 Caveat: Switching straight to enforcing on a host that has run without SELinux can
                   break services. Use permissive first and read the denials.
                 Commands (review before running):
                   # review first; a system that has run disabled needs a relabel:
                   sudo fixfiles -F onboot
                   # set SELINUX=permissive in /etc/selinux/config, reboot, review denials, then set enforcing
